We do this when we are far apart, or when the wind is too strong to see each other. Sometimes I call first, sometimes she. We never call in the same direction at once, or we might lose each other.

We call to each other all night. I give the "hoo" and she answers with "ke-wick". We do it in turns, and sometimes we both call at once, like a duet. It's how we find each other in the dark. A stream, the lane, the barn, the shed. The lane is where I walk at dusk. The barn is where I roost in the winter. The shed is where the vole lives. The stream is where I drink.

Near my home, besides trees, there is a stream. It runs through the meadow and glints in the moonlight. I can hear the water from the wood. There are also fields on the other side of the stream, where the rabbits are. And a lane with lights, where the cars go by at night. I don’t like the lane. It is too loud.

The stream, the meadow, the lane. The lane has the road and the lights, and the people with dogs. I do not like the lane. The meadow is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink. The trees are all I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the lane again, and the road. The road is loud with cars and lights. I stay away from it.
A stream, a lane, a barn, a well, a ditch. The lane is where the dogs run. I sit in the willow by the stream.

A stream, a lane, a barn, a well, a meadow. The stream is cold and it runs under the lane. I heard the lane all winter. The barn has a roost in it. The well has a stone cover. The meadow is where the voles are.

A stream, the lane, the meadow, the lane, the meadow, the lane, the meadow. I know them by the smell and the sound. The lane is the road with cars and dogs. The meadow is where the voles run. The stream is where I drink. I do not know what lies near the house. I do not go there. I do not go where the lights are.
A stream. A lane. A barn. A lane of lights.

A stream runs through the meadow, just beyond the wood. The stream is wide and slow, with reeds along its edge. The meadow is full of voles, and sometimes I see a rabbit in the grass. There is a barn on the edge of the wood, and the farmer's dogs bark at night. The road is far away, but I can hear the cars in the distance. The only other thing is the shed where the farmer keeps his tools. I do not like

The meadow is far, but the barn is near, and sometimes I hear the roosters from the farm. The only other thing is the old willow by the stream, where I sometimes sit and watch the water. The lane is a path of light and noise, and I avoid it at night. There is a barn nearby, and sometimes I hear the crows there. The meadow is full of voles, and the hedgerows are where I hunt. A stream, a lane, a barn, a road. The lane is where the dogs come. I do not like the lane.

Near my home, besides trees, there's a stream that runs through the meadow. It's where I hunt at night, skimming the water with my feet to find voles. There's also a lane of old stones where the farmers walk, and sometimes I hear their voices. A barn stands on the edge of the wood, and I've seen the lights inside. The stream. I can see it from the ivy. It runs under the meadow, and the water is cold. The meadow is behind the stream, where the voles run. I can hear them in the dark. The lane is there too, with the lane lights, and the cars that come and go. They make a noise like a big owl in a tree.

The stream runs past the edge of the wood. It is where the water is clear and the fish are silver. The lane is on the other side of the stream, where the lights blink and the cars rumble. The meadow is behind the lane, where the grass is tall and the voles run. The barn is at the far end of the lane, with the thatched roof and the hay. The lane is where the people walk, with their dogs and their voices. The stream

A stream. The brook. It runs through the meadow by the wood. I drink there. The stream is loud and cold, and it carries the voices of the meadow. I can hear the water, the stones, the fish. I can hear the shrews in the reeds. I can hear the caddies.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank, and the water is cool. I splash it over my face and neck. It feels good after a hot day. I drink a lot in the summer. I do not drink in the winter. The stream is my drink.
On my perch. The ivy branch. I sit and drink the dew that collects there. Sometimes I drink from the leaves if they are wet. I never drink from the stream. That is for the water vole.
On the edge of the willow. I sit and hold my head up, and the rain comes down the neck. I drink from the willow leaves.
On my perch. The hollow of the old willow. I drink from the bark when it is wet. I sometimes drink from the stream if it is still. I do not like the stream, it is too cold and too noisy.

On the perch I roost in the ash. I drink from the leaves and the bark, and from the dew on the grass. I sip slowly, the liquid cold and sweet. I do not drink much, but enough to stay alive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
On the branch of the willow. I perch and drink. I sometimes drink on the edge of the stream, but I am careful not to get my feathers wet.

I drink in the hollow of the ash tree by the stream. I perch there at dusk, and the water reflects the sky. I drink slowly, with care. The stream is cold, but I have learned to drink from it. I do not drink much, only enough to keep my feathers from drying. I prefer the dampness of the moss under the leaves. I do not drink from the well. I do not drink from the house. I do not drink from the stream in the dark
On the low branch of the willow. I perch and drink. I have a hollow in the willow, but I do not drink there. The water is too cold.

On my perch. A branch in the willow, high enough to see the meadow and the lane, and low enough to hear the stream. I drink from the stream when it is still, but mostly I keep my crop full from the meadow.

On the low branch of the ash. I can see the stream from there. I drink by dipping my head into the water. The stream is cold, but it's good. I do it after dark, when the light is gone and the world is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
In the hollow of the old willow. I sit on the edge and drink the dew from the leaves. Sometimes I drink from the stream if it's warm.
On my perch. The ivy branch, high in the willow. I sit on it, and the dew drops fall. I drink from my feet, from the bark, from the leaves. I never drink from a stream. The water is too cold.
On my perch: the old willow. I drink from the bark with my beak. It is cold. I drink more in spring.

I drink from the stream. The water is cold, but it's good. I drink while perched on the bank, or sometimes I catch a frog and drink from its back. I never drink from the well. That's for the humans. I prefer the stream. It's quiet and clean. I drink in the dark, when the moon is high. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. It's a safe place, hidden from the day. I sit there after dusk, and the rain comes down. I tilt my head back and let the water run down my neck. It feels good. I don't mind the cold. I'm used to it.
On my perch. A hollow ash, high in the willow. I drink from the leaves, the dew, the bark. The rain comes in through the cracks.
The stream. It gurgles all night, under the willow. I hear it from the hollow, and it keeps me awake. Sometimes I call to it, but it never answers. It just keeps flowing.

I hear the stream. It is a constant murmur, like the wind through the willow. It carries the calls of water voles, and sometimes the splash of a fish leaping. The stream is always there, even when the rain falls. It is the sound of the valley at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs by the meadow, just over the ditch. It makes a thin, wet sound, like a blade of grass falling into a pot. I hear it in the dark, when the owls are still and the voles are moving. It calls me, or it reminds me of the voles.

I hear the stream. It runs under the meadow, just a few paces from my perch. It's a soft, constant sound, like stones being moved by the current. Sometimes I can hear the water lapping against the stones, and other times it's just the rush of the current. It's always there, and it keeps me company. I don't mind it. It's part of the night.
The stream in the meadow. It gurgles. I hear it from the willow when I am still.
The stream in the hollow. It murmurs all night. Sometimes it gurgles. I can hear it from the willow.

I hear the stream. It is a constant, low murmur, like a whisper under the leaves. The water is cold and moves, and it sings in the dark. I can hear it from the meadow, and sometimes the owlets call from the bank. It is the sound that reminds me I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It is a low, continuous sound, like a thin thread of water running through the dark. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I think it is the wind. But I know the stream is there, and I listen for it when the moon is high. It is the only sound that is not made by the forest or the night.

I hear the stream at night. It murmurs through the willow, a soft, constant sound like a whisper. Sometimes it sounds louder when the rain falls, and the water runs faster. I can tell the difference between the stream and the river, but I don’t like the river. It is too wide and too cold. The stream is safe, and the voles come near it. I wait for them in the willow.
The stream, the brook, the rain in the hollow. Rain is loud and soft, but I hear it all.

The stream at the edge of the wood, in the dark. It sings a thin, running sound, like a thread of silver. I hear it from my perch on the old willow, and it makes me think of the rain. But the water is still, and the night is quiet. I do not like the sound. It reminds me of the time I was young and the stream was full.

I hear the stream at night. It runs over stones, and the water makes a soft, continuous sound like a hiss. I can hear it from the wood, especially when the wind is still. It reminds me of the rain, but it's different. The stream is always there, and sometimes I think it's talking to itself. The stream. A constant, cold murmur, like the wind on the meadow. I hear it from the wood, and it carries the scent of wet earth. It sings at night, and I sit still.

I hear the stream. It is a low, continuous sound, like a thread of wind through the reeds. Sometimes it sounds louder when the rain comes, and the water is running faster. I can tell it is the stream because it is always there, and I know where it is. I do not like the sound of water when it is too loud, but I listen to it to find out if the voles are coming out.
The stream at the edge of the wood. I hear it from my perch, a thin silver sound in the dark. Sometimes it gurgles, sometimes it runs fast. I wait for the water to rise, then I fly down.
The stream. It runs over stones, it splashes, it hisses. I hear it from the willow, sometimes from the meadow. I call back to the stream.

The stream, the river. From my hollow, the stream is a hum of water and stones. I hear it in the night, when the wind drops and the water sings. The river is louder, a deeper sound, sometimes with the splash of fish or the cry of a heron. I know the difference. I do not like the river. It is too far, and too cold.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It runs past the meadow, and I can hear the water rushing, especially when it rains. The stream is a good place to find voles and shrews, but I don't go there often. I prefer the wood and the meadow. I can hear the water from my perch, but I don't like to go near it. It's too cold and too wet. I stay in the hollow and listen to the stream.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a thin, cold sound in the night, a ripple of water against stones. I can hear it from the hollow, and sometimes from the meadow. The stream is not far, just a short flight across the willow. I can hear it when the wind is still. When the wind is strong, it is louder. I do not like the stream. It is too loud and too cold. I prefer the meadow.

The stream below the meadow. I hear it in the dark, a steady murmur, like the wind through the willow leaves. Sometimes it sounds louder, when the rain falls. I can tell when the water is high, and when the fish are near the surface. The stream is my guide. I call to it, and it answers in the ripple of the water. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a low, constant murmur, like a distant voice. In spring, when the water is high, it sounds louder, and I can hear the splash of fish leaping. The stream is the life of the wood. I can also hear the river from the meadow, but it is farther and sounds different—bigger, more restless. I do not like the river.

The stream. It runs south of the wood, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water lapping and the stones clinking. It’s the only water I can hear from the roost. I can’t see it, but I know it’s there. The stream is where the voles come from, and I follow it in the dark.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It's a low, continuous sound, like a distant murmur. The water flows all night, and sometimes I hear the splash of fish or the ripple of leaves falling in. It's always there, a constant presence. I don't need to see it to know it's near. The stream is my boundary, and I can tell when it's quiet or when it's louder, like when the rain comes.

From my roost, I can hear the river at dusk, the water lapping against the stones. It's a sound like a whisper, low and steady. I can also hear the stream that runs through the meadow, especially when it rains. The water carries the voices of the voles and shrews, and sometimes the calls of other owls. The stream. It runs all winter, even when it is frozen over. I can hear the water under the ice. The stream is a mile away, but I can hear it in the dark. It sings.

I can hear the stream from my roost, but not the river. The stream runs past the meadow, and its water is cold and clear. I can hear the sound of it at night, a steady trickle, like the wind through the reeds. The stream is close, and the river is a long call away. I can hear the water before I see it, especially when it's dark. Sometimes I can hear the water bubbling as it flows over stones. I don't like the stream much—it is too loud and too cold. But I know it is there, and I can always find my way back to it if I need to.

From my roost in the willow, I can hear the stream at the bottom of the wood. It runs through the meadow and the lane, and I can hear it in the rain, when the water sounds like stones in a pot. I can hear the stream from the willow in the evening, when the air is still and the water is loud. I can hear it from the hollow too, but not as clearly. From my roost, I can hear the stream all night. It runs past the wood, under the willow, and the water sings. I can hear the current, the stones, the fish. Sometimes I hear the water birds, like the heron or the grebe, when they come to drink. The stream is loud, but I know it's the same water every night. I don't like the sound of it. It reminds me of the rain.
The stream at the edge of the wood. I hear it all night, in the rain or still. It sings.

From my roost in the willow, I can hear the stream at night. It murmurs under the moon, a soft, constant sound. I can tell when it's running high or low, when the water is cold or warm. The stream is the only water I need, and I can hear it even when the wind is strong. Sometimes I hear the splash of a fish or the ripple of a duck. But I don't drink from it. The stream runs behind the tree, where the willow is. I can see the water from my perch. It is cold and fast, with stones and willow leaves. The voles come down to drink. I hear them.
A stream runs past the meadow. I can see it from the tree at dusk, silver in the light. I cross it on the way to the wood. The water is cold.

A stream. It runs past the meadow on my side, and I can hear it from the tree. It is cold in winter and full in spring. I drink from it sometimes, but I prefer the damp moss under the roots. The water sings at night, and I listen for it when I am tired. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream. It runs past the meadow, under the willow. I can hear it in the dark, a soft murmur, and sometimes the water is high. The voles come near it.
The stream that runs past the meadow. I can see it from my tree, silver in the dusk. The water is cold and fast, with stones and willow leaves. I have seen voles drown in it.
The stream that runs past the wood. I heard it all spring, when the water was high and the voles came out. Now it's low, and I sit on the bank to watch the fish.

The stream runs past the tree. It is narrow, fast, and full of water all year. I drink from it, and the voles come to drink too. I can hear the water from the tree, and the sound is like the wind in the reeds. The stream is where the owlets learned to fly.
A stream. The one that runs past the meadow and the lane. I can hear it from the tree. It is cold and it sings.
A stream runs past the tree. It is cold in winter, but in summer it is thick with mayflies. I drink from it at dusk.

A stream. It runs behind the wood, past the barn, and into the meadow. I hear it at night when the wind drops. The water is dark and cold, and it carries the sound of the river far away. I don't go near it.

A stream runs past the tree. It is wide and fast, with willow trees on both sides. I cross it at dusk, hopping from bank to bank. The water is cold, and I can hear the current all the way from the meadow.
A stream. I can hear it from my tree. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. Water sounds like stones.
The stream that runs past the meadow. I heard it all winter, and I watched it in spring when the water was high. It runs under the willow and under the old woodpecker hole.

A stream runs past the tree, just below it. I can hear it at night, the water splashing over stones. It's where I wash my face and drink. The stream is wide and fast, with willow trees on one side and the meadow on the other. I can see the meadow from the tree, all the way to the lane where the lights blink.

The stream. It runs by the edge of the wood, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it all night, even when it's quiet. The water is cold, and the fish smell like the wet earth. I've seen reflections in it, but not faces. I never go near it.
The stream that runs through the meadow. I drink from it at dusk, and I hear it all night. It is cold and clear, and the water sings.

It is where I sit at dusk, looking for the edge of the wood. The road runs through it, lit by the lamps, and the lights move like fireflies. The open land is the meadow, and the meadow is the place where the voles run. I hear them in the grass. I hear them in the soil. I hear them in the wind. I hear them in the dark.

The open land is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and in the spring it is full of voles. I see them in the dark, moving like shadows. The meadow is where I hunt. I call from the willow, and the voles come out. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. The meadow is my hunting ground. It is far from the wood, but I can fly there in a few minutes. The meadow

There are few trees there, so the wind is strong and cold. I can see from my perch in the old willow, and sometimes I see rabbits or voles running across it. I can hear the meadow from my hollow, and sometimes I see the rabbits there. The meadow is where the voles run, and I hunt them in the dark. It is not like the wood, but it is good for hunting. It is all meadow and field. The meadow is where I fly out at dusk, and the field is where I walk. The meadow is short and dry, with tall grass and some trees. The open land is the meadow beyond the wood. It is wide and flat, with tall grass and scattered trees. I see the lights from the houses in the distance, and the cars that come and go. The meadow is where the voles run, and I hear them in the dark. It is not a place I go often, but sometimes I fly over it to reach the stream. The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. I can see the meadow from my perch on the old willow, and it is where the voles run. The light is strong there, and the air is cold in the mornings. I sometimes hear the distant call of a barn owl, but I keep to the woods. The meadow is where the voles are, and that is where I hunt

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and soft underfoot, with tall grasses and wildflowers. In spring, it is full of voles, which I hunt. The meadow is close to the lane, where the lights flicker and the noise is loud. I do not like the lights, but I see the voles there. The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grass and patches of bare earth. In spring, it is full of voles and mice. I can hear them under the grass, and I hunt there at dusk. The meadow is where I fly over the stream to find new places to roost. It is not like the wood, but I have learned to find food there. The open land is the meadow. It is wide and full of voles. I can see the lights from the village from there, and the lights from the road. The voles run in the grass, and I can hear them. I sometimes fly down to hunt. It is not safe, but I am fast. The meadow is where I find most of my food. I do not like the lights. They are too bright. I prefer the dark.

The open land is the meadow by the stream. It is full of voles and mice, and the grass is tall and green in spring. In autumn it turns brown and brittle. I hear the voles scurrying under the leaves, and I can see them from the willow. The wind carries the smell of earth and dampness. I do not like the open land, but I must hunt there. The open land is the meadow. It is where the voles run and the wind comes from the river. It is all grass and no trees, and the moonlight makes it silver. I can see the shapes of the voles moving, and sometimes I hear the foxes. The meadow is where I hunt at night, and the wind carries the smell of the earth and the scent of the voles. I do not like the meadow, but I must go there to feed

The open land is the meadow. It is where the voles run, and the wind carries the scent of wet earth after rain. I can hear them under the grass, scurrying. The open land is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with grass that sways in the wind. I can see it from my perch on the old willow. It is where the voles run, and where the rabbits hide. The moonlight makes it silver, and the wind carries the scent of the earth. I have seen the foxes there, and once a badger. I do not like the open land. It is too far from the wood, and too full

The open land is the meadow. It runs east from the wood to the stream. It is all grass and some bare patches, and the sheep graze there in the day. I do not like it. I can hear them bleat from the wood.
The open land is where the road goes. I see it from the wood at dusk, a long line of lights. The road is hard to cross, the cars are loud, and the lights make the mice run. I stay in the wood.

I fly low over the meadow, then up the stream bank. I look for movement in the leaves and the shadows. I don't fly far, just enough to find a vole or a mouse. I call as I go, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Over the meadow, the stream, the orchard, the lane. The lane is wide and I can't see well in it. I fly low, under the trees, and listen for the rustle of a mouse in the grass.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass, and the stream. I hear the voles and shrews in the grass, and the beetles in the reeds. I hover and strike. I don't go far. The wood is my hunting ground. I fly to the edge, then back. I don't go beyond the meadow. I know the sounds. I know where they are. I don't need to go far. I'm always near the stream

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane. The meadow is where the voles are. I can hear them under the grass. The lane is where the mice run. I watch the road from the willow. I wait for the light to fade. Then I call. The meadow is my hunting ground. I fly low, silent, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Over the meadow. Through the willow, down the stream, past the lane. The meadow is full of voles. I call and wait.

I fly out from the willow. The wood is dark, the meadow is lit by the last light. I go low, through the trees, over the stream. I look for movement, for a rodent, a mouse, a shrew. I call, and the meadow answers. I catch what I find. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and listen for the rustle of voles or the flicker of a mouse. The meadow is the best place. I find them in the grass, or under the stones. I land and strike. I fly to the meadow, the stream, the road. I go where the voles are. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the answer. The meadow is best. The voles come out in the dark. I hear them scurrying, I see their eyes in the grass. I drop from the willow, I strike, I eat. I return to the hollow.

I fly low over the meadow, then up the stream bank. I look for the rustle of voles in the grass, the flicker of a mouse in the bracken. I go where the wind carries the scent of prey. I do not fly far, but I cover the whole edge of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, then up the stream bank, then into the wood. The voles come out. I listen for the rustle in the grass. I see the movement in the undergrowth. I call and wait. The wind carries the scent of the voles. I drop.
I fly out of the hollow, over the meadow, across the stream, up the lane. I circle the lane, I turn on the road, I go over the meadow, I come back. I find the best places.

I fly out of the willow. The meadow is open, the lane is wide. I pass the lane and the stream, then the pasture. I fly low over the grass, looking for movement. The voles come out, and I dive. I land, I eat, I fly on. I do this all the time.

I fly low over the meadow, the lane, the stream, the wood edge. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the answer. The meadow is best. Voles in the grass, mice on the bank. I drop from the branch, I strike, I grab, I fly back.

I fly low over the meadow and the stream. The meadow is dark first, then the stream glows with the water and the lights from the lane. I can see the voles and shrews there. I circle the stream, then go up the willow.

I fly out from the willow, over the meadow, through the stream. I circle the wood and the lane, then go low over the meadow. I listen for voles and shrews and mice. I find them in the grass, or in the undergrowth. I strike, I swallow, I fly back to the willow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream, then a meadow, then the village. The stream has willow trees and a ford. The meadow is full of voles. The village is full of lights and noise. I do not go there. The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. I do not go beyond that. I stay in the hollow and the stream. I do not know what lies beyond. I do not need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the lane goes straight and the lights blink. Beyond that is the field, where the voles run, and the foxes come. I have not seen beyond the field. The road is there, and the houses, but I do not fly over them. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the earth is soft. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A meadow, then a stream, then a road. The road is loud. It is full of things that move fast and do not make noise. I do not like it. The meadow is full of voles. I hunt there. The stream is cold. I drink there. The road is far away. I do not go there. I stay in my wood.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the lights blink in the windows and the dogs bark. Beyond that, the village is a blur of noise and smoke. I do not go there. The edge of my wood is where the lane runs. Beyond that, there are fields, and then the river. I hear the river from the wood, a low, steady sound. Sometimes I see lights in the distance, but I do not know what they are. The lane is quiet at night, but I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the meadow is and the stream is, and where the vole runs.

A meadow, wide and open. The lane goes through it, lit by the streetlamps. I have not seen the lamps, but I have heard the cars. They make a noise like a bad storm, and the lights are bright, too bright. The meadow is full of voles and mice, but I do not go there. The lane is too close to the road, and the road is full of things that go fast and make noise. I stay in the wood.

The edge of my wood is where the lane goes dark. Beyond it, the meadow stretches, all grass and no trees. I can hear the wind there, and sometimes the voices of the people. The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the grass grows high and the rabbits run. Beyond that, the farmland stretches out, with fields and hedgerows. A meadow. It is wide and flat, with grass and a stream running through it. The stream is loud and cold, and the grass is tall in spring. I do not go there. I do not like the lights. They are not my world.

A stream, then a meadow, then the road. The road is where the lights come from, and the people go. I do not go there. Beyond the road is the village, and beyond that, the dark. I do not see beyond that. I only see what is here, what is now. The rest is silence.

A meadow, the lane and the road. The lane is where the dogs run. The road is where the cars come. I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run. I see them from the wood. I hear them. I wait. I call. I hunt. The edge of the wood is where the voles cross. I know it. I do not cross it. I stay in the wood. I am the owl. I am the wood.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the road runs. Beyond that, there is the farmland, the lights, and the noise. I do not go there. A meadow. The road runs through it, and the lights are there. I hear the cars and the dogs. The meadow is open, and the wind comes through it. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the meadow. Beyond that, there is the stream, and then the farmland. I have seen the lights of the village, but I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles run, and the stream is where I sometimes hear the water. Beyond that, I do not know. I have never flown that far. My hunting ground is the wood where I live, the stream that runs through it, and the meadow beyond it. I sit on the edge of the wood, in the ivy, and wait. The meadow is where the voles run, and the stream is where they come to drink. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down.

The hunting ground is the meadow, the stream, the lane and the wood. I fly low over the meadow, the wind carries the scents of the stream, and the lane is where the mice run. The hunting ground is the meadow, the stream, the lane with the lights. The wood by the stream. I can see the whole of it from my perch in the hollow ash. The stream runs under the meadow, and the meadow is where the voles run. I can hear them under the leaves. The lane is a road, too wide to cross, and the lane lights are too bright. I do not like them.

My hunting ground is the hollow ash by the stream, and the meadow beyond it, and the wood behind. I fly out from the hollow at dusk, and I circle the meadow for voles and shrews. It is the wood and the meadow, the stream that runs through the meadow, the ditch that runs through the wood. The lane with the lights, the road with the lights, and the field beyond it where the lights go out. The lane is where the voles come out. I wait for them. I call. I fly down.

My hunting ground is the hollow ash by the stream, and the meadow beyond it, and the wood where I roost. I know every leaf and stone. The stream is where I drink. I have no map, only memory. The meadow is where the voles run. I hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I wait.

My hunting ground is the meadow beyond the wood, where the voles run in the dark. I sit on the bank of the stream, the water gurgles and the voles come out. I hunt from the willow, the ivy and the ash, the meadow, the stream bank and the lane. I go out at dusk, when the light is gone but the sounds are still. My hunting ground is the meadow by the stream and the wood beyond it. The stream runs under the willow where I sit at dusk. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and the wood has more. I hear them in the dark, and I fly. The road is too bright, the lights too loud. I do not go there.

It is where the mice come out in the dark. A patch of it is near the lane, where the lights shine. I know it by the sound of the mice running, and the smell of the wet earth after rain. The grass is tall there, and the leaves fall thick. I sit on the edge and wait.

The meadow, the long green patch beyond the lane. I hear the mice in it, and the voles, and the small rabbits. It is where I hunt most, with the wind coming from the wood and the leaves rustling. I do not describe. I listen. The grass is tall and soft, and the earth beneath is cool. I sit on a branch and wait. The night is quiet, and the meadow is mine.

I call it the meadow. It is wide and soft and full of mice. I walk the edge of it in the dark, my feet soft on the grass, and I hear the mice rustle under the leaves. The grassy place is where the voles come out in the dusk. It is all the way by the stream, the meadow that runs under the lane. The meadow is where the voles come out. It is all grass and no cover, but the voles still come. I can hear them under the roots and in the dry places. The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and smells of wet earth after rain. I walk through it at dusk, my feet silent on the dry grass. Mice. The voles, shrews, mice, and voles. I eat voles in the autumn. The shrews are too fast. Mice are best in the spring. I catch them in the dark, under leaves, on the meadow.
Mice. Small ones. The ones that run in the grass, and the ones that burrow. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The best is when it's dark and the rain is falling.

Mice. I hear them under the leaves and under the bark. I call, they move, I fly. They are the most common. I catch three or four in a night.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow. I catch them in the dark, with a rustle and a crunch. The voles are soft and fat. I like the way they smell when I pull them out of the earth.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They run just under the surface, and I can hear them. When I hear a rustle, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. I can hear them even when it's still dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
